article.title: Creator marketing as a system, not one-off campaigns
article.desc: One-off creator campaigns reset every time. How founders can engineer creator marketing as one compounding system across content, distribution, credibility and performance.
article.intro: You are not running campaigns. You are running fragments. A creator post here, a launch push there, and every new brief starts from zero.

sections.p: Each one-off campaign has its own creators, its own message and its own metrics. Nothing carries over, so the brand never builds the familiarity that makes audiences trust it.

Treat creator marketing as one engine: content creators genuinely want to make, distribution that reaches the right audiences, credibility built by consistent voices, and performance measured across the whole programme rather than post by post.
Fragments only become a whole through real understanding: of your audience, of the creators who speak to them, and of what each part of the system is for. Map that first, then scale what works.
Start with the next three months: fewer and longer creator relationships, one shared narrative, and one view of performance for the whole system.

article.close: Talk to us about engineering your creator programme as one system.

persona.t: Max Harper is the Growth Catalyst — a founder who treats marketing, technology and the creator economy as core to growth, and wants systems that compound, not campaigns that reset. That is exactly the problem here.

pain.t: Marketing content for founders rose from 3 to 32 a month into an April peak, yet peers frame it as one system only 3% of the time — WHITESPACE. Read the rise as directional; the prior year is unverified.

angle.t: The fragmentation angle names what Max keeps being told — that creator marketing is a string of one-off campaigns, a view the peers reinforce. Show the pieces first and the case for one system makes itself.

insight.t: This story is credible because it is Vamp's own thesis. Saying creator marketing is one engineered system, not a pile of campaigns, is something no peer says — and it is Aaron's to own.

ship.t: Lead with 'Your story, told by those who truly get it.' This pillar carries 60% of the quarter, so it sets the rhythm — TOFU names the fragments, MOFU proves the system, BOFU books the consultation.

article.title: After the conference: turning event contacts into relationships
article.desc: The best conversation at the conference is often the one nobody follows up on. How founders can turn one week of events into a year of real relationships.
article.intro: The best conversation at the conference was the one nobody followed up on. Events like Cannes bring the industry together for a week, then everyone flies home and the momentum disappears.

sections.h: Speed creates the illusion of connection
sections.p: Back-to-back meetings, parties and panels feel productive. But a handshake and a swapped contact are not a relationship. Real connections take time, and events rarely leave room for it.

sections.h: Build the home that events don't
sections.p: Founders need an always-on place to keep conversations going: a curated community, regular small gatherings and shared projects that give people a reason to talk again.
Within a week, send one useful thing to every person you want to stay close to. Within a month, invite them to something small. Within a quarter, find a way to work together.
Speed might attract, but depth wins hearts. One week at an event can become a year of relationships if you design for what happens after it.

article.close: Build the community that outlasts the conference.

persona.t: Max is motivated by business success, recognition and genuine connection. A founder community that keeps going after the event speaks to something Max already values, not a need you have to invent.

pain.t: Peers touch networking and events in 18% of their content, but nobody owns what happens after the event. The deck rates it EMERGING, rising from February to June — present, unowned and claimable.

angle.t: The fast-pace angle fits because events compress everything into a week — the industry connects intensely at Cannes, then goes quiet. Question the speed and the need for an always-on home becomes obvious.

insight.t: Vamp can tell this story because it already lives it — it runs a 100,000-creator community all year, not just in event week. 'Connection takes time' is something it practises, not only says.

ship.t: Lead with 'Slow down. Build connections that matter.' This pillar takes 25% of the quarter — TOFU recalls the follow-up that never happened, MOFU turns one event week into a year, BOFU invites founders to apply.

article.title: Will AI replace creators? An honest read for founders
article.desc: AI is not replacing creators. It scales the repetitive half of the work while humans earn the trust. A practical look at where each one wins in creator marketing.
article.intro: Founders keep hearing that AI will replace creators. It makes a good headline and a poor guide to what is actually changing in creator marketing.

sections.p: AI is excellent at the repetitive half of the work: research, briefs, variations, scheduling and reporting. Used well, it gives teams more time and more options.
Trust comes from a recognisable person with a point of view. Audiences follow creators for their judgement, taste and honesty, and none of that scales by copying them.
The strongest programmes put AI underneath the creators, not in place of them: AI for scale, humans for trust. Decide which tasks each one owns before you buy another tool.
Innovate with a clear head, not a hype cycle. Test AI on one workflow, measure what it saves, and keep the human voice at the front.

article.close: Get the honest read on AI in creator marketing.

persona.t: Max treats technology as core to growth and wants an honest read on AI — neither panic nor a sales pitch, just a plain account of what it actually changes for a founder.

pain.t: Monthly tech and AI content in the founder cohort spiked to 16 in April, but the AI-in-creativity strands are still nascent and mostly unclaimed — EMERGING frontier ground with low competition.

angle.t: The AI-misconceptions angle starts from what founders keep hearing — that AI will replace creators — and corrects it plainly. You are not adding to the noise, you are explaining what it gets wrong.

insight.t: Aaron can tell this story because Vamp builds the tech itself. 'AI for scale, humans for trust' carries more weight from someone who ships the tools than from someone commenting from the side.

ship.t: Lead with 'Innovate with a clear head, not a hype cycle.' Keep this pillar to 15% of the quarter — TOFU says AI scales the boring half, MOFU states the split plainly, BOFU offers the full read.

why.t: Aaron Brooks is near-silent across 12 months of founder-audience content while five peer founders publish steadily — absent from the conversation he is most qualified to lead.
